**Why this matters**

The CPU performance equation splits a program's run time into three factors: how many instructions it executes, how many clock cycles each one takes on average (CPI), and how long a cycle lasts. Any claim that a processor, a compiler flag or a rewrite is faster is a claim about those factors, and the equation is how you check whether a gain in one was paid for in another. <plan>
- Why copying the sign bit keeps the value
- Zero extension, and which of the two C picks
- Widening the narrow fields inside an instruction

In an $n$-bit two's complement pattern the top bit has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and every other bit a positive weight. Take the 4-bit pattern 1001: $-8 + 1 = -7$. Widened to 8 bits it is 11111001. The old low bits 001 still give $+1$. The five ones above them give $-128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = -8$, exactly the weight the old top bit had, so the value is still $-7$. For a value that is not negative the copies are zeros and add nothing.

<note>Sign extension: to widen a two's complement value, copy its top bit into every new bit. The ones from the old top bit upwards add up to the old top bit's weight: $-128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = -8$ when 4 bits become 8.</note>

**Why this matters**

Gray code orders binary patterns so that neighbouring values differ in exactly one bit. Absolute rotary encoders use it to report the position of a shaft, asynchronous FIFOs use it for the read and write pointers that cross between two clock domains, and Karnaugh maps use it for their row and column order. A fixed-point number is an integer with an agreed scale. In Q4.4 the stored integer is the value times $2^4 = 16$: 2.5 is stored as 40 and 1.5 as 24. Addition needs nothing special, because both operands carry the same scale: 40 + 24 = 64, and 64 / 16 = 4.0.

<note>Fixed point: stored integer = value × $2^f$, where $f$ is the number of fraction bits. Q4.4 has $f = 4$, a scale of 16. Stored integers add and subtract directly, because both sides carry the same scale.</note>

**Problem 1 · warm-up**

In Q4.4, 2.5 is stored as 40 and 1.5 as 24. Which integer should be stored for the product 2.5 × 1.5, and how do you get it from 40 and 24?

<solution>40 × 24 = 960 carries the scale twice (16 × 16 = 256). Divide by 16 once, a right shift by 4: 960 >> 4 = 60. As a value, 60 / 16 = 3.75 = 2.5 × 1.5.</solution>
<check lang="python">
assert 2.5 * 16 == 40 and 1.5 * 16 == 24
assert (40 * 24) >> 4 == 60 and 60 / 16 == 2.5 * 1.5
</check>

The fault is the scale, not the width of the register.</grade>

A TLB entry holds one translation: a virtual page number and the physical frame it maps to. A hit gives the frame at once; a miss means the translation has to be fetched from the page table first, which costs several memory reads.

<note>TLB: a small cache of page translations (virtual page number → physical frame). A hit avoids the page-table lookup; a miss pays for it.</note>

<ask type="short">A TLB has 64 entries. A loop repeatedly reads one byte from every page of a 512 MiB buffer, and the buffer is mapped with 2 MiB pages. How many pages does the loop touch, and can all of their translations stay in the TLB?</ask>

One entry maps one whole page, whatever the page size, so the memory a TLB covers at one time is its entry count times the page size. That figure is the TLB reach. With 4 KiB pages, 64 entries reach 64 × 4 KiB = 256 KiB: a loop that stays inside 256 KiB can have every translation in the TLB, and one that ranges over more has to keep evicting entries and fetching them again.

<note>TLB reach = number of entries × page size. 64 entries of 4 KiB pages reach 256 KiB.</note>

history.tutor:
A calling convention is the agreement that lets separately compiled functions call each other: where the arguments go, where the result comes back, and which registers a call is allowed to overwrite.

<ask type="short">Under the System V x86-64 convention, `f` holds one value in `rbx` and another in `r10`, then calls `g`. After `g` returns, which of the two values can `f` still rely on, and whose job was it to keep that value intact?</ask>

reply:
The registers are shared: `g` runs on the same sixteen general-purpose registers as `f`. The convention settles who protects what by putting each register into one of two classes. A caller-saved register may be overwritten by any call, so a caller that still needs its value has to save it before calling. A callee-saved register must hold the same value on return as it did on entry, so a function that wants to use one has to save it first and put it back before returning. The class of each register is fixed by the convention, not chosen by the function.

<note>Caller-saved register: any call may destroy it; the caller saves it if it still needs the value. Callee-saved register: a function that uses it must put the old value back before returning, so a caller can rely on it across a call.</note>

<ask type="short">Suppose a convention makes register A callee-saved and register B caller-saved, and `g` wants to use both as scratch space. What must `g` do for A that it need not do for B?</ask>

Check 1 covers every position whose number has the 1s bit set (1, 3, 5, 7), check 2 those with the 2s bit set (2, 3, 6, 7), and check 4 those with the 4s bit set (4, 5, 6, 7).

<note>Hamming(7,4): parity bits sit at positions 1, 2 and 4. The check for parity bit $p$ covers every position whose binary number contains $p$: check 1 covers 1, 3, 5, 7; check 2 covers 2, 3, 6, 7; check 4 covers 4, 5, 6, 7.</note>

It has the 4s bit and the 2s bit but not the 1s bit, so it is covered by checks 4 and 2 and not by check 1. If bit 6 alone is flipped, exactly those two checks fail and check 1 still passes. Every position has its own set of checks, because every position has its own binary number.

Two kinds of event make the CPU stop what it is doing and enter the kernel. An interrupt comes from outside the running instruction stream: a device or a timer signals the CPU, and it can arrive between any two instructions. An exception is caused by the instruction being executed, such as a division by zero or an undefined opcode, so it happens at the same point every time the program runs with the same data.

<note>Interrupt: asynchronous, raised by a device or timer, unrelated to the current instruction. Exception: synchronous, raised by the instruction being executed (divide by zero, undefined opcode, a breakpoint).</note>

learner.question: wait so where does a segfault fit in this? is it an interrupt, or is it just the OS deciding to kill me

reply:
It starts as an exception. When an instruction reads or writes an address that has no valid mapping, or one the process may not use in that way, the CPU's memory management unit raises a fault on that instruction: it is synchronous, so by the definition above it is an exception, not an interrupt. The kernel's handler then finds that the access cannot be put right and sends the process the SIGSEGV signal, whose default action is to terminate it; "segmentation fault" is the message the shell prints for that. So the hardware raises the exception and the operating system decides what follows.

reply:
<grade verdict="correct" score="1">"it's 1 when an odd number of the inputs are 1" is the whole specification of the sum bit: the low bit of a count is its parity.</grade>

Now find the gate. XOR of two bits is 1 exactly when they differ, and for two bits that means exactly one of them is 1: an odd count. So $a \oplus b$ reports whether the number of ones in $a$ and $b$ is odd. A second XOR with $c$ leaves that answer alone when $c = 0$ and flips it when $c = 1$, and one more 1 is exactly what turns an odd count into an even one and back. The sum bit is therefore $a \oplus b \oplus c$, reached from the counting argument and not from a memorised table.

<note>Full adder sum bit: $s = a \oplus b \oplus c$. It is the low bit of the count of ones among the three inputs, so it is 1 when an odd number of them are 1. Each XOR brings one more input into the parity.</note>

In a ripple-carry adder each column has to wait for the carry from the column below it, so the top bit of a 32-bit sum is not settled until a carry has had time to pass through all 32 columns. Faster gates inside each column do not change that, because the waiting is in the chain and not in the column. The way out began with a different question: how much can a column say about its carry out from its own two bits, $a$ and $b$, before any carry in has arrived.

<note>Ripple-carry delay grows with the width: the carry into the top column has passed through every column below it.</note>

<continue/>

reply:
Take the columns one kind at a time. If $a = 1$ and $b = 1$, the column's count is already 2 before any carry in is added, so its carry out is 1 whether the carry in turns out to be 0 or 1. That column does not need to wait: it generates a carry by itself. If $a = 0$ and $b = 0$, the count can be at most 1 even with a carry in, so the carry out is 0, again with no waiting.

<note>Generate: a column with $a = 1$ and $b = 1$ has a carry out of 1 whatever its carry in, so $g = a \land b$. A column with $a = b = 0$ has a carry out of 0 whatever its carry in.</note>

<plan>
- The serial part as a limit
- Speedup for a given core count
</plan>

Amdahl's law: if a fraction $p$ of a program's run time can be spread over $n$ cores and the rest cannot, the speedup is $S = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + p/n}$. With $p = 0.5$ and $n = 2$: $S = 1/(0.5 + 0.25) = 1.33$.

<note>Amdahl's law: $S = \frac{1}{(1-p) + p/n}$, with $p$ the parallel fraction of the run time and $n$ the number of cores. As $n$ grows, $S$ approaches $\frac{1}{1-p}$.</note>

**Problem 1 · warm-up**

A job takes 100 s on one core. 90 s of that is work that parallelises perfectly; 10 s is serial. How long does it take on 9 cores, and what is the speedup?

<solution>The serial part stays 10 s. The parallel part takes 90 / 9 = 10 s. Total 20 s. Speedup = 100 / 20 = 5.</solution>
<check lang="python">
t = 10 + 90 / 9
assert t == 20 and 100 / t == 5
</check>

<ask type="problem">The time on 9 cores and the speedup, with your steps.</ask>

learner.answer: Easy. 9 cores means 9 times faster on the 90% that's parallel, so 0.9 × 9 = 8.1x speedup. Time is 100 / 8.1 = 12.3 s.

reply:
<grade verdict="wrong" score="0.1">"0.9 × 9 = 8.1x speedup" multiplies the parallel fraction by the core count, which treats the 10 s of serial work as if it took no time. The serial part runs for its full 10 s however many cores there are.</grade>

Work in times, not factors. The serial 10 s is unchanged. The parallel 90 s is shared by 9 cores: 90 / 9 = 10 s. The total is 10 + 10 = 20 s, so the speedup is 100 / 20 = 5, not 8.1.

<card>Why is the speedup not the parallel fraction times the core count? :: The serial part keeps its full run time. Add times: T(n) = serial + parallel / n, then speedup = T(1) / T(n).</card>

<note>Amdahl by times: new time = serial time + parallel time / n; speedup = old time / new time. The fraction is never multiplied by n.</note>

**Problem 2 · same idea**

A job takes 60 s on one core: 12 s serial and 48 s perfectly parallel. Find its run time on 4 cores and the speedup.

<solution>Serial 12 s. Parallel 48 / 4 = 12 s. Total 24 s. Speedup 60 / 24 = 2.5.</solution>
<check lang="python">
t = 12 + 48 / 4
assert t == 24 and 60 / t == 2.5
</check>

<ask type="problem">The run time on 4 cores and the speedup, as serial time plus parallel time.</ask>

A ripple-carry adder adds two binary numbers one bit position at a time, starting from the least significant bit. Each position adds three bits: one from each number and the carry in from the position to its right. It writes the low bit of that sum and passes the high bit on as the carry out. For 0110 + 0111: bit 0 adds 0 + 1 + 0 and writes 1; bit 1 adds 1 + 1 + 0 = 10, writes 0 and carries 1; bit 2 adds 1 + 1 + 1 = 11, writes 1 and carries 1; bit 3 adds 0 + 0 + 1 and writes 1. The result is 1101, which is 6 + 7 = 13.

<note>Ripple-carry addition: at each bit, s = a + b + carry in; write s mod 2 and carry out s div 2. Each carry out is the next position's carry in, so the top bit waits for every carry below it.</note>

<continue/>

| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 11 | 1 | 1 |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

Follow each Carry out into the Carry in of the row below it: that hand-off is the ripple, and the sum bits read from the bottom row up give 1101.
